title: The Claude-Native Law Firm: How I Actually Practice Law with AI in 2026
author: Zack Shapiro

dom.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI should reshape legal-service delivery rather than merely accelerate isolated tasks. It adds a concrete practitioner example in which AI supports subscription pricing and broader service within a predictable fee, while preserving lawyer verification, judgment and responsibility. It does not directly resolve Harvey’s durability or vertical-vendor competition.
qs: AI makes this model work, because I can deliver more comprehensive service within a predictable fee structure.

But the judgment, the part where you decide what to fight for and what to concede, where you read between the lines, where you make a call that could go either way and stake your reputation on it, that is yours.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: Shapiro materially develops the cluster’s proposition by showing how a configured general-purpose Claude interface can encode lawyer-specific procedure and produce usable legal deliverables, while preserving attorney judgment and verification. His concrete workflow and timing claims support platform pressure on specialist tools, but remain first-person anecdotes rather than proof of autonomous practice or general superiority.
qs: For a small firm practitioner, a well-configured general-purpose AI is better.
To be clear: every document that leaves my firm has been reviewed, revised, and approved by a licensed attorney.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition and adds a concrete practitioner case: supervised AI has expanded a small firm’s capacity, reduced the document-production rationale for associate hiring, enabled hybrid subscription pricing, and increased the premium on judgment and verification. Its evidence is firsthand and unquantified, so it illustrates rather than establishes broader structural change.
qs: The work that traditionally justified an associate hire, first-pass document review, research memos, initial drafts, redline summaries, routine correspondence, is now handled by Claude under my supervision.
To be clear: every document that leaves my firm has been reviewed, revised, and approved by a licensed attorney.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: Shapiro accepts the platform-shift and commoditisation thesis and materially extends it with first-person evidence that a technically capable small firm can configure Claude directly for legal workflows rather than use specialist legal-AI products. His account also reinforces the cluster’s qualification that agentic production still requires lawyer verification, although his performance comparisons remain practitioner assessments rather than controlled findings.
qs: For a small firm practitioner, a well-configured general-purpose AI is better.
I then review every citation, stress-test the analysis, and revise where my judgment diverges from the output.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition and adds a concrete first-person implementation account: AI restructures a small firm’s staffing and task allocation, enables predictable subscription pricing alongside hourly billing, and preserves attorney supervision. Its evidence is experiential rather than comparative or independently measured, and it does not directly establish market-wide bargaining shifts toward legal departments, ALSPs or AI-native providers.
qs: The work that traditionally justified an associate hire, first-pass document review, research memos, initial drafts, redline summaries, routine correspondence, is now handled by Claude under my supervision.
AI makes this model work, because I can deliver more comprehensive service within a predictable fee structure.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts selective augmentation, insisting that lawyers interrogate AI outputs and retain strategic judgment and responsibility. It materially extends the cluster through concrete practice-level implementation: AI-assisted drafting stress tests, confidentiality controls, client consent, attorney supervision and AI-enabled subscription pricing. Its productivity claims are practitioner anecdotes rather than measured evidence, and it does not address junior development or staffing leverage.
qs: The research on this is consistent: people who use AI outside its competence, or who trust it without interrogating the output, perform worse than people who don’t use AI at all.

But the judgment, the part where you decide what to fight for and what to concede, where you read between the lines, where you make a call that could go either way and stake your reputation on it, that is yours.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition and adds a concrete small-practice operating example: AI performs supervised first-pass production, while lawyers retain judgment, client relationships, verification and responsibility. It also illustrates hybrid hourly/subscription pricing and instruction-driven workflow design, although the evidence is self-reported rather than independently evaluated.
qs: And what you need them to do has changed: judgment, client relationships, and AI output supervision, not 2,000 hours of document production.
To be clear: every document that leaves my firm has been reviewed, revised, and approved by a licensed attorney.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core task-substitution/complementarity proposition and materially develops it with a practitioner account: AI performs supervised first-pass work, enabling a two-person firm to handle greater capacity while shifting associate value toward judgment, relationships and verification. It also illustrates business-model adaptation through hybrid hourly and subscription pricing, though its productivity claims remain anecdotal rather than measured.
qs: The work that traditionally justified an associate hire, first-pass document review, research memos, initial drafts, redline summaries, routine correspondence, is now handled by Claude under my supervision.
But the bar for when hiring one makes economic sense has moved.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core premises through practitioner testimony: AI now performs supervised first-pass work that traditionally justified associate hiring, while verification, judgment and final responsibility remain with experienced lawyers. It also anticipates associates shifting toward judgment and AI supervision. However, it does not directly examine how juniors will acquire that judgment or propose the cluster’s deliberate training responses.
qs: The work that traditionally justified an associate hire, first-pass document review, research memos, initial drafts, redline summaries, routine correspondence, is now handled by Claude under my supervision.
And what you need them to do has changed: judgment, client relationships, and AI output supervision, not 2,000 hours of document production.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core supervised-aid model: AI can improve drafting efficiency and quality, but remains under attorney supervision and established confidentiality duties. It also endorses concrete provider diligence, data controls and client consent. Its stronger optimism about prompting and eventual professional expectations does not displace human accountability.
qs: The provision frames AI as an efficiency and quality enhancer, emphasizes attorney supervision, ties data handling to existing confidentiality obligations, and secures client consent.

Your obligations are to make reasonable efforts to protect client data, which in practice means turning off model training on your inputs, understanding the provider’s data handling practices, and documenting your reasoning.

kp.k: AI expands small-firm capacity against larger competitors
kp.d: Writing in 2026, Shapiro describes a two-person transactional boutique handling startup formation, venture capital transactions and regulatory work. Based on his own practice over the preceding year, he claims AI enables faster, more thorough work at a cost structure unavailable 18 months earlier. His acquisition anecdote reports core analysis in under two hours; the comparison with three associates working until morning is his estimate, not a measured comparison.
qs: I run a two-person boutique law firm. We handle startup formation, venture capital transactions, and regulatory work.
A team of three associates at a mid-size firm would have needed until morning to produce that analysis. I had the core of it in under two hours.
It moves faster, produces more thorough work product, and operates at a cost structure that would have been impossible 18 months ago.

kp.k: General-purpose models challenge specialized legal software
kp.d: Shapiro argues that a well-configured general-purpose model is superior for his small-firm practice to specialized products including Harvey, Spellbook, CoCounsel and Luminance. He characterizes those products as foundation-model wrappers and claims direct access to frontier capabilities avoids vertical vendors' engineering delays. These are his comparative judgments from evaluating tools, rather than reported benchmark results.
qs: For a small firm practitioner, a well-configured general-purpose AI is better. It’s not close.
The specialized products are wrappers built on top of the same foundation models that power the general-purpose tools.
When you’re on the frontier model, every new capability ships to you on day one. When you’re on a wrapper, you’re waiting for someone else’s engineering team to decide what to build next.

kp.k: Individual judgment, not templates, drives customization value
kp.d: Shapiro treats template libraries as commodity inputs and argues that useful customization encodes the individual lawyer's issue-spotting, risk prioritization, communication style and analytical framework. Persistent Claude skills operationalize those instructions automatically. He proposes the same architecture for litigation, tax and family law, while identifying his own experience as transactional.
qs: A template library is not a competitive advantage.
Those instructions encode an individual lawyer’s judgment, not a firm’s template library.
I’ve created custom instruction files, called “skills,” that encode my analytical frameworks, my preferred formats, my voice, and my judgment about how specific types of legal work should be done.
I’m describing my own practice here, which is transactional. But nothing about the architecture is practice-specific.

kp.k: Code generation integrates analysis with document production
kp.d: Shapiro reports using Claude's coding capabilities to manipulate Word files at XML level, generate attributed tracked changes, preserve formatting and standardize citations. He argues this bridges legal analysis and finished work-product production without opening Word or Litera, and claims specialized legal AI cannot match the capability.
qs: These are not legal problems. They are software problems. And Claude solves software problems by writing software.

When I tell Claude to apply tracked changes to a contract, it doesn’t use a plugin or a macro. It opens the .docx file at the XML level and writes the exact markup that Microsoft Word expects, attributed to my name, preserving every formatting detail.
They give you a chatbot that talks about documents. Claude is a system that can reach inside those documents and change them.

kp.k: Different modes allocate different levels of task autonomy
kp.d: Shapiro distinguishes conversational Chat, where he controls each step, from Cowork, which reads, creates and edits files while deciding how to execute assigned tasks. He uses Cowork for full redlines and closing-document generation. Code provides terminal access; his reported use includes building a document-to-audio pipeline to accommodate difficulty reading long documents.
qs: I stay in control of every step.

I point Claude at a folder on my computer, give it a task, and it goes and does it. It reads files, creates new ones, edits existing documents, and makes its own decisions about how to get from A to B.
But I have a condition that makes it hard to read long documents, so I used Code to build a command-line tool that converts legal documents into spoken audio.

kp.k: Transferable skills could accelerate transmission of professional knowledge
kp.d: Shapiro reports developing six skills over a couple of hours after Claude identified recurring patterns across months of conversations: contract review, tracked changes, drafting, client communications, research and policy writing. He hypothesizes that distributing the resulting plugin to 50 associates would immediately standardize their first drafts around his framework, voice and formatting. He presents this as faster transmission of knowledge traditionally conveyed through mentorship, while retaining attorney review.
qs: By the end I had six production-ready skills bundled into a single plugin for the Cowork desktop app: contract review, tracked changes editing, contract drafting, client communications, legal research, and policy writing.
If I had 50 associates, I could install it on every machine.

Knowledge that takes years of mentorship to transmit is now an instruction file that works from the first draft. The output still requires attorney review, but the review starts from a much higher baseline.

kp.k: Contract workflows combine automated review with human negotiation judgment
kp.d: In a reported 40-page counterparty-redline workflow, Claude classifies severity, identifies risk shifts and cross-provision tensions, checks missing provisions and proposes counter-language. Shapiro selects positions using relationship and deal context, authorizes edits and reviews every change before sending. He reports a response package in under an hour, including about 30 minutes of his own thinking.
qs: Claude organizes every change by severity, flags where the counterparty shifted risk, identifies tensions between modified provisions, checks for standard provisions that should be present but aren’t, and produces a summary with specific counter-language for each issue.
I pick the one that accounts for relationship dynamics and deal context that no AI has access to.
I review every change, and I send it.
Total time from receiving the markup to having a response package ready to send: under an hour, of which about 30 minutes is my own thinking.

kp.k: Research combines parallel searches, self-review and attorney verification
kp.d: Shapiro describes parallel regulatory research prioritizing primary authority, followed by model self-review for citation support, uncertainty and contradictions. He reports first drafts in under an hour versus his estimate of days for a junior associate, then personally checks every citation and stress-tests the analysis. Although he labels the workflow 'Research without hallucinations' and attributes fake-citation incidents to inadequate quality control, he supplies no measured hallucination rate or study establishing elimination of errors.
qs: My research skill instructs Claude to launch parallel research across every relevant angle simultaneously rather than working through them sequentially: the securities analysis, the state licensing requirements, the banking regulations, the consumer protection implications.
Claude must verify that every cited authority actually says what the memo claims. It must flag anything where its confidence is below high. It must check for internal contradictions across sections.
The problem was never AI itself. It was AI without quality control.
Claude delivers a first draft in under an hour. I then review every citation, stress-test the analysis, and revise where my judgment diverges from the output.

kp.k: Real-time cross-checking supplies a second-reviewer function
kp.d: In a client dispute with 48 hours to respond, Shapiro reports that Claude matched allegations against the agreement and correspondence, identifying two of four alleged breaches as involving obligations modified by a side letter. During drafting it also flagged a proposed defense that could concede a payment-dispute point. He presents this anecdote as a second-lawyer checking function embedded in the drafting conversation.
qs: Claude mapped every factual allegation in the demand letter against the specific contract provisions cited, and found that two of the four claimed breaches referenced obligations that had been expressly modified by a side letter the counterparty’s own counsel had drafted.
It caught one: a defense I was planning to raise on the service-level metrics could have been read to concede a point on the payment dispute in Section 7.
That kind of real-time, provision-by-provision stress-testing while actively drafting is something that used to require a second lawyer reviewing your work.

kp.k: Confidentiality requires provider diligence, safeguards and client consent
kp.d: Shapiro asserts that existing third-party technology frameworks and the agent/instrumentality exception apply to AI, attributing this position broadly to ABA guidance and state ethics opinions without identifying specific authorities. He recommends disabling training, understanding data handling and documenting the decision; cites Anthropic's zero-data-retention API option and business agreements; and reports obtaining consent through engagement-letter provisions emphasizing supervision and confidentiality. He predicts non-use will become harder to defend professionally, rather than establishing a current duty to adopt AI.
qs: ABA guidance and state bar ethics opinions treat AI tools as third-party technology providers covered by the agent/instrumentality exception.

Your obligations are to make reasonable efforts to protect client data, which in practice means turning off model training on your inputs, understanding the provider’s data handling practices, and documenting your reasoning.
The provision frames AI as an efficiency and quality enhancer, emphasizes attorney supervision, ties data handling to existing confidentiality obligations, and secures client consent.
We are approaching the point where not using these tools is the harder professional responsibility position to defend.

kp.k: Detailed persistent instructions underpin useful first-pass output
kp.d: Shapiro argues that generic requests yield mediocre results whereas instructions specifying client perspective, market norms, missing provisions, severity, counter-language and negotiating constraints produce useful first drafts. Skills make that specificity reusable. His adoption recommendation is to start with a frequent task and encode how it should be done; he claims this requires a few hours learning the tool rather than technical expertise.
qs: The entire gap between “AI is a toy” and “AI changed my practice” lives in the quality of your instructions.
This is why skills matter: they encode that level of detail so you write it once and it fires every time.
Closing that gap doesn’t require technical skill.

kp.k: Automation raises the economic threshold for associate hiring
kp.d: Shapiro says Claude now performs supervised first-pass review, research, drafting, redline summaries and routine correspondence that traditionally justified associate hiring. He does not predict associates becoming obsolete, but argues their economic justification and expected work shift toward judgment, relationships and AI-output supervision. Every outgoing document in his practice remains reviewed, revised and approved by a licensed attorney.
qs: The work that traditionally justified an associate hire, first-pass document review, research memos, initial drafts, redline summaries, routine correspondence, is now handled by Claude under my supervision.
To be clear: every document that leaves my firm has been reviewed, revised, and approved by a licensed attorney.
Associates are not obsolete. But the bar for when hiring one makes economic sense has moved.
And what you need them to do has changed: judgment, client relationships, and AI output supervision, not 2,000 hours of document production.

kp.k: AI supports subscriptions alongside hourly billing
kp.d: Shapiro reports passing some time savings to clients while using other efficiency gains to deepen analysis within the same hours. His firm offers both hourly billing and flat monthly subscriptions covering advisory work, contract review, compliance monitoring and routine governance. He attributes subscription viability to AI-enabled capacity, describing predictable revenue and clients' greater willingness to seek advice without a running meter.
qs: The point is not that every task takes less time. It is that every hour of attorney time produces more value.
My firm offers subscription pricing alongside traditional hourly billing, depending on the engagement.
The subscription clients get ongoing advisory, contract review, compliance monitoring, and routine governance for a flat monthly fee.
AI makes this model work, because I can deliver more comprehensive service within a predictable fee structure.

kp.k: Experienced judgment remains essential despite automation
kp.d: Shapiro warns against stopping checks or using AI beyond its competence. He invokes unspecified research claiming such use can worsen performance relative to non-use, without providing study details. His central position is supervised augmentation: the lawyer remains responsible for strategic choices and final work. He predicts that 10 or 20 years of accumulated practice judgment becomes more valuable when combined with AI.
qs: The research on this is consistent: people who use AI outside its competence, or who trust it without interrogating the output, perform worse than people who don’t use AI at all.
The lawyers who will win with this technology understand at a foundational level that the AI is not practicing law. You are practicing law.
If you’ve spent 10 or 20 years developing judgment in your practice area, you are sitting on exactly the asset that AI makes more valuable, not less.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shapiro claims that AI enables a two-person boutique to compete with much larger firms through faster, more thorough work and a lower cost structure.
pts.d: He describes his startup, venture-capital and regulatory practice as already achieving these advantages in 2026. His acquisition anecdote attributes rapid cross-document issue identification and negotiation support to Claude; the comparison with three associates is his estimated counterfactual, not a measured comparison.

pts.k: Shapiro claims that a well-configured general-purpose model is superior to specialized legal-AI products for a small-firm practitioner.
pts.d: He attributes the advantage to personalized instructions, direct document manipulation through generated code, and immediate access to frontier-model improvements. He characterizes specialized products, including Harvey, as wrappers and argues that template-based firm customization addresses a less important source of value than individual professional judgment. These are his product and market assessments.

pts.k: Shapiro claims that persistent, transferable instructions can encode a lawyer’s working methods and raise colleagues’ first-draft quality.
pts.d: He reports building six skills covering review, editing, drafting, communications, research and policy writing. He predicts that distributing the plugin across a hypothetical 50 associates would transmit his analytical framework, voice and formatting preferences immediately. This is a claim about transferring working methods and improving the review baseline, not eliminating attorney review or demonstrating equivalent professional judgment.

pts.k: Shapiro claims that agentic workflows automate document production and provide rapid research and real-time analytical support.
pts.d: He describes Cowork as autonomously reading, creating and editing files and choosing execution steps. Reported examples include a response package to a 40-page markup in under an hour, a regulatory research first draft in under an hour, and cross-provision stress-testing that previously required a second lawyer. He also reports using Code to build a document-to-audio tool accommodating his difficulty reading long documents. The workflow remains attorney-supervised rather than direct reliance on autonomous final legal advice.

pts.k: Shapiro claims that AI raises the economic threshold for associate hiring and shifts the work firms need associates to perform.
pts.d: He says Claude now performs supervised first-pass review, research, drafting, redline summaries and routine correspondence that previously justified hiring. He explicitly rejects associate obsolescence, instead predicting greater emphasis on judgment, relationships and supervision of AI output. He further argues that accumulated experience becomes more valuable.

pts.k: Shapiro claims that AI increases value per attorney hour and makes subscription services economically workable.
pts.d: He distinguishes tasks whose time savings he passes to clients from tasks receiving deeper analysis within the same hours. His firm combines hourly engagements with flat monthly subscriptions for advice, contract review, compliance monitoring and governance. He attributes more predictable revenue and clients’ greater willingness to contact counsel to this model, rather than claiming that hourly billing disappears.

pts.k: Shapiro presents quality-controlled AI use as compatible with professional obligations and predicts that non-use will become harder to defend.
pts.d: He attributes citation failures to inadequate quality control and describes automated self-checking followed by his own citation verification and substantive review. He also argues that existing third-party technology and confidentiality frameworks accommodate AI, subject to data diligence, supervision and client consent. His prospective professional-responsibility claim is not presented as an already universal requirement to adopt AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is Shapiro’s reported practice experience, concrete work anecdotes and self-reported task times.
pts.d: He recounts an acquisition negotiation, a contract-redlining workflow, regulatory research and a commercial breach response. The breach example describes discovering side-letter modifications affecting two of four allegations and avoiding a defense that could undermine a payment position. His broader competitiveness, quality and staffing conclusions extrapolate from his own two-person practice. The document supplies no systematic productivity dataset, independently assessed output-quality results, comparative benchmark or quantified cost accounts.

pts.k: Product comparisons and transferability claims rest on personal evaluation and extrapolation; research and ethics claims invoke unspecified external authority.
pts.d: Shapiro says he evaluated most specialized tools but provides no evaluation protocol or comparative results. His 50-associate deployment is hypothetical. He invokes research on performance deterioration from inappropriate AI reliance without identifying studies, and ABA guidance and state ethics opinions without citing particular opinions. He references sanctions over fabricated citations without naming cases and does not report a measured hallucination rate or establish a zero-error outcome.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims describe current practice in 2026, with recent retrospective comparisons and undated near-term predictions.
pts.d: Shapiro situates the transformation over the preceding year and compares the cost structure with 18 months earlier. The acquisition episode occurred a few months before publication. Reported speed gains concern particular tasks, not universal turnaround guarantees. Predictions about Cowork’s impact, diffusion to other practices and professional expectations have no specific deadline.

pts.k: The claimed benefits depend on detailed configuration, task-appropriate use, experienced judgment, human verification and data safeguards.
pts.d: Shapiro argues that a few hours spent learning modes and building reusable instructions can unlock the workflow without technical skill. He conditions useful first passes on detailed instructions and retained lawyer decision-making. Automated self-review is a preliminary quality-control step distinct from his subsequent human verification. For confidential material, he identifies disabling training, understanding provider practices, documenting decisions and obtaining consent; he mentions specific API and business arrangements rather than demonstrating identical settings across every product mode.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries and disrupted roles are small transactional firms, their clients, associates, experienced lawyers and competing providers.
pts.d: Shapiro’s direct examples concern a two-person boutique serving startup, venture-capital, acquisition, commercial and regulatory matters. Small firms gain capacity relative to large competitors; associates face changed hiring economics and task expectations; experienced lawyers gain a way to amplify their judgment; clients may receive savings, deeper analysis and predictable subscription fees. Firm managers could distribute standardized working methods. Specialized legal-AI vendors face his claimed general-purpose-model advantage. He extends the architecture to litigation, tax and family practice as a proposed application, not reported experience. The source does not establish an access-to-justice outcome.
